title: Normal Distribution
body:
The bell curve. Symmetric about $\mu$, unimodal, with tails that never quite reach zero:

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}
$$

Nobody memorises that. What matters is that it has exactly two parameters, **$\mu$ locates it and
$\sigma$ scales it**, and that changing them slides and stretches one fixed shape rather than
producing a different curve. Mean, [[Median]], and [[Mode]] all sit at $\mu$, because it is
symmetric.

## Why it is everywhere

Not because nature likes bells. Because of the [[Central Limit Theorem]]: **sums and averages of
many independent contributions go normal regardless of what they were summed from.** Heights,
measurement errors, and total demand are all sums of many small independent effects, so they
inherit the shape. Anything built by multiplying instead of adding goes log-normal and is skewed,
which is why incomes are not bell shaped.

The practical consequence is that $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal even when the data is not, and
that single fact is what blocks 3 and 4 of [[STATISTICS]] run on.

## Standardising

$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, and any normal becomes the **standard normal**
$Z \sim N(0,1)$. **All normal tables are one table**, and the $z$-score is a unit-free statement:
"this observation is 2.3 standard deviations above the mean", comparable across quantities measured
in different units entirely.

The reason the table has to exist at all is that $\int e^{-x^2/2}dx$ has no elementary
antiderivative. There is no formula for the normal CDF, only numerical values, which is unusual
enough to be worth knowing. See [[Probability Density Function]].

## 68-95-99.7

| Within | Probability | Outside |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu \pm 1\sigma$ | 68% | about 1 in 3 |
| $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ | 95% | about 1 in 20 |
| $\mu \pm 3\sigma$ | 99.7% | about 1 in 370 |

Worth memorising, because it turns a standard deviation into an intuition and it is the whole
reason $\alpha = 0.05$ became conventional: two sigma is the round number nearest "unusual". The
precise multiplier for 95% is $1.96$, and that number appears in every $z$-interval in
[[Confidence Interval]] and every two-sided test in [[Hypothesis Testing]].

Beyond three sigma is rare enough that manufacturing quality control names itself after it, and it
is also where the normal model is least trustworthy: real data has fatter tails than the curve
predicts, so extreme events are consistently more common than a fitted normal says. That is the
standing criticism of normal-based risk models.

## Working with it

```
Scores are normal with mu = 500, sigma = 100. P(X > 650)?

z = (650 - 500)/100 = 1.5
P(Z > 1.5) = 1 - F(1.5) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668
```

Every problem is that: convert to $z$, look up a CDF, subtract from 1 or take a difference. Going
the other way (a percentile to a value) is $x = \mu + z\sigma$ with the $z$ read out of the table
backwards.

Linear combinations stay normal, which nothing else in the family table does: if $X$ and $Y$ are
independent normals then $aX + bY + c$ is normal, with mean $a\mu_X + b\mu_Y + c$ and variance
$a^2\sigma_X^2 + b^2\sigma_Y^2$. That closure property is what makes the algebra in block 3 work
out so cleanly.
